title: Does Parenthood Really Ruin Couples’ Sex Lives?
author: Wendy Wang
source: Institute for Family Studies (ifstudies.org), November 5, 2026, November 6, 2026
summary: Wendy Wang uses General Social Survey data from 2021 to 2024 to test whether parenthood kills a couple's sex life, prompted by a viral essay claiming it did. She finds that married childless couples no longer have the edge they once did: similar shares of parents and non-parents report weekly sex, and 17 percent of childless adults versus 15 percent of parents had little or no sex in the past year. Young parents have sex slightly less often than childless peers, but the pattern reverses in middle age, and the gap widens after 50. The sharper decline in the past decade has been among childless couples under 50, part of a wider American sex recession. A regression shows that age, family income and religious attendance predict a sexless marriage, while having children, education and political ideology do not. Weekly sex is linked with higher marital happiness, and Wang concludes that parenthood is not likely the culprit.
points: Married parents and childless couples now report similar rates of weekly sex, ending the slight edge childless couples once held.
Young married parents have sex somewhat less often than childless peers, but the pattern reverses in middle age and the gap grows after 50.
Weekly sex among married adults has fallen from 61 percent to 46 percent since the 1990s, part of a broader sex recession.
Age, family income and religious attendance predict a sexless marriage, whereas having children does not.
Couples who have weekly sex are far more likely to say their marriage is very happy than sexless couples (70 percent versus 42 percent).
quotes: For quite some time, married childless couples had a slight edge in the sex department over their peers with children, but this is no longer the case.

Even though young married parents (ages 25 to 34) have sex less often than young married adults without children (62% vs. 65% weekly), the pattern reverses during middle age, and the gap is much bigger after 50.
It is important to note that America is in a “sex recession,” as previous IFS research showed that the share of American adults who have regular, weekly sex is at a record low.
As to which couples are more likely to be in a sexless marriage, the data points to three significant factors: age, income, and religious attendance.
Nearly 1 in 5 married adults ages 25 to 64 who never or rarely attend religious services (18%) are in a sexless marriage, compared with 13% of the married adults who attend services regularly.

A number of factors are not significantly associated with the odds of being in sexless marriage, including whether married adults have children or not, education (college vs. non-college educated), and political ideology.
But one thing seems clear from these findings: parenthood is not likely the culprit for a sexless marriage.
